title: PlugMem: A Task-Agnostic Plugin Memory Module for LLM Agents
one_liner: This paper gives agents a reusable memory plugin that stores distilled knowledge instead of long raw histories.
lead: An agent that works over many sessions needs long-term memory, but raw logs become too large and too unfocused. This paper studies a memory module that stores compact pieces of reusable knowledge rather than copying full trajectories back into context on every task.

problem.h2: Raw memory logs grow fast and return too much irrelevant detail
paras: A long-lived agent can remember every conversation, tool trace, and web trajectory, but replaying all that text on later tasks floods the context with detail that does not matter. The agent then spends effort on irrelevant history instead of the few facts and rules that the current task actually needs.

Task-specific memory systems avoid some clutter, yet they do so by baking in assumptions about one benchmark or one task family. The paper asks for a memory design that stays reusable across tasks while still retrieving information that is sharply tied to the current decision.

callout.html: Store compact actionable knowledge instead of full raw histories, because later tasks usually need the lesson from an experience rather than the whole transcript.

panels.title: 1. The agent accumulates many experiences
panels.viz_args: Conversations, web tasks, and retrieval episodes keep piling up.
panels.caption: A raw memory store quickly becomes too large to reuse directly.

panels.title: 2. Raw replay returns clutter
panels.viz_args: Whole histories come back, even when only one small lesson matters.
panels.caption: The context budget is consumed by detail that does not guide the next decision.

panels.title: 3. Distill each experience into knowledge
panels.caption: The system saves factual statements and procedural rules extracted from experience.

panels.title: 4. Retrieve only the relevant pieces
panels.viz_args: The current task pulls back a small set of related knowledge items.
panels.caption: This keeps the returned context compact because the unit of access is distilled knowledge.

panels.title: 5. The next decision uses dense memory
panels.viz_args: The agent acts with a short list of relevant facts and rules.
panels.caption: The target is better memory use because the retrieved content is more concentrated.

steps.text: Take a trajectory from conversation, retrieval, or web action.
Turn that trajectory into factual statements and action rules so that the lesson is separated from the full raw transcript.
Place those knowledge items into a structured memory graph so that related facts and rules can be reached together.
Pull back only the small subset of knowledge that matches the present task.
Use the distilled items to guide the next action or answer.

paras: The paper changes the unit of memory access. Instead of retrieving long raw episodes, it retrieves distilled knowledge items that summarize what the agent should carry forward.
object.object: the memory unit returned to the agent

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: information density of retrieved memory
hidden.name: how much task-relevant guidance is contained in each returned unit of memory
paras: The paper focuses on information density: how much useful guidance a returned memory item carries relative to its size. A raw transcript may contain the right lesson, but it also contains greetings, dead ends, and other local detail.

High information density matters because the agent has limited context space. If each retrieved item carries more decision value, the agent can see the useful lesson without dragging in the rest of the past session.

heat.caption: The darkest cells show where the gain comes from: dense knowledge items that survive across tasks and use less context space.

reads.html: The best memory item is short but carries a lesson the current task can act on immediately.
Distilled knowledge raises information density, which means the agent can retrieve fewer items while still bringing back the facts and rules that matter.

paras: A knowledge-centric memory can work because most later decisions do not need a full replay of the past. They need the retained fact, the useful caution, or the action rule that past experience revealed. Distilling memory into those units makes retrieval more selective.

The linked memory structure also matters because facts and rules often support each other. A rule such as 'check account region before billing changes' is more useful when it is connected to the fact that region settings are stored in a specific page. Returning linked items can give the agent a tighter decision packet than a flat raw history would.

stages.s: Extract compact facts and rules from the experience
Store those items with links to related items
Retrieve only the small task-matched subset
Dense memory for the next decision

math.words: Memory usefulness rises when the returned content carries more task-relevant guidance per unit of context space.
symbols: how useful the retrieved memory is for the current task
the amount of factual or procedural help the returned memory provides
how much room the returned memory occupies in the prompt

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a raw trajectory uses 100 lines of context and only 10 of those lines directly guide the current task.
Under this rough view, its memory_value is 10 divided by 100, which is 0.10.
Suppose a distilled memory packet uses 20 lines and still carries those same 10 useful guidance lines.
Then memory_value is 10 divided by 20, which is 0.50.
The example shows why distillation matters because the same guidance becomes much easier to reuse when the extra history is removed.

math.note: This ratio is a teaching device. The paper's real message is that compact retrieved knowledge can outperform long raw replay because it carries the needed lesson without the surrounding clutter.

charts.title: Raw episode retrieval
charts.note: Raw replay wastes context space because each retrieval drags in local details that the current task does not need.

charts.title: Distilled knowledge retrieval
charts.note: Distilled retrieval lifts reuse and lowers clutter because the memory unit is a compact lesson rather than a full session log.

items.b: The distillation step throws away a needed detail.
items.html: If a memory rule omits the page condition that made the rule valid, the agent may reuse the lesson in the wrong situation.

items.b: The memory store becomes too abstract.
items.html: If all experience is compressed into vague rules, the agent may lose the concrete facts needed to apply those rules correctly.

items.b: Retrieval links pull in the wrong neighbors.
items.html: A linked memory structure can still add clutter if the related items are only loosely connected to the current task.
The method works when each stored item keeps the concrete fact or rule that will matter later and retrieval remains narrow enough to fit the current decision.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build an agent that handles several task families, such as long conversation support, multi-step retrieval, and web action tasks. Compare two memory systems: one that retrieves raw past episodes and one that retrieves distilled knowledge items. Measure context length, accuracy on repeated tasks, and transfer to a new task family that still shares some underlying facts or action rules.

The demo proves the paper's point if the distilled memory system matches or exceeds task success with less retrieved context, because the returned memory carries more relevant guidance per unit of prompt space.
demo.closing: A strong demo should include one task where the useful lesson is buried inside a long old transcript, because that is the situation this memory design is meant to fix.
